1:
Henry opens on motive rather than masonry. It is of great consequence in all our religious actions that we design well and that the eye be single; had Solomon built this house in the pride of his heart, as one eastern king made a feast only to display the riches of his kingdom, it would not have turned to his account at all. But the king states his inducements, and Henry finds them such as not only justify the undertaking but magnify it.

There are three. The first is the glory of God, which Henry calls the highest and ultimate end: the house was for the name of the Lord God of Israel, to be a habitation for him. He handles the paradox of the opening verse carefully — God has, so far as we are concerned, made darkness his pavilion, so let this house be the residence of that darkness; it is in the upper world that he dwells in light no eye can approach. The second is that God had already chosen the city. Jerusalem was full of stately buildings for the king and the royal family, and Henry draws the inference plainly: if God has chosen the place, it is fit that the building raised for him should excel all the rest, and if men are so honoured there, let God be honoured so. The third is filial — Solomon was carrying out what his father had intended and never had opportunity to do.

Ellicott works the same verses as a textual critic, comparing them throughout with the parallel account. The opening claim he would render with the emphasis the Hebrew carries, and I on my part have built; the corresponding phrase in the older book, which doubles the verb, seems to him the original, and he notes which ancient versions follow it. Two words in the sentence he marks as poetic — one of them occurring only five times in all — and he judges that a conjunction inserted before the second weakens the parallelism the line was built on.

The details accumulate in the same manner. One verse he reports as standing word for word with the parallel; in another the only difference is a singular where this text has a plural, and he observes that the unpointed Hebrew of the older passage could be read either way. Where this chapter says the people were brought out of Egypt, the parallel says the people Israel, and the Syriac and Arabic supply the name here too, as those versions often follow it. He adds that some manuscripts omit one of these six verses altogether.

The largest divergence is a whole clause about God choosing no ruler, which the older account does not contain. Ellicott resists treating it as a late insertion: there is nothing in its language against the supposition that it belonged to the earlier text from the first. And he draws one sharp point out of it. The statement that God had chosen no man to rule glances at Saul, who was the people's choice rather than God's, and Ellicott takes the occasion to say that Scripture nowhere teaches the voice of the people to be the voice of God.
9:
The promise given to David is quoted with its refusal intact, and Ellicott hears the emphasis fall on the pronoun: only thou, thou shalt not build. He notes that the Hebrew says for thy son where the English says but, and that apart from that the verse stands as in the older account. Wesley takes the same refusal and turns it outward. Thus one sows and another reaps — and let not the wisest of men think it any disparagement to carry on the good designs that those before them had laid.

Ellicott continues verse by verse in the same manner. The word for establishing the promise he renders literally as causing it to rise up; spoken means promised, and set means seated. Where this text says the ark was placed in the house, the parallel says a place for the ark was placed there, and Ellicott records that the Syriac and Arabic keep the fuller form. What the ark contains he identifies without hesitation as the two tables of the law.

Henry stands at the point where the prayer begins and describes what has just happened. Solomon had signed and sealed the deed of dedication, appropriating the house to the honour and service of God; now he prays the consecration-prayer, and by it the temple is made a figure of Christ, the great Mediator through whom all our prayers are to be offered and from whom all God's favours are to be expected. Wesley says the same thing in almost the same words, that in every matter where we have to do with God we are to have an eye to him.

What Henry then does is gather the doctrine the prayer assumes. First, that the God of Israel is of incomparable perfection: we cannot describe him, but we know there is none like him in heaven or earth, for all creatures have their fellow-creatures and the Creator has no peer. Second, that he is true to every word he has spoken, so that those who set him always before them and walk before him with all their hearts find him as good as his word and better. Third, that he is infinite and immense, whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, and to whose blessedness nothing whatever is added by the utmost we can do in his service. Fourth, that he alone knows the hearts of men, all their thoughts and aims and affections lying naked and open before him.

The posture of the prayer gets Ellicott's closest attention, because the verse describing it has no counterpart in the older book. He judges that it may once have stood there, since nothing in it bears the marks of the chronicler's own style. The platform he renders literally as a pan — it looked, he says, like a laver turned upside down, and was doubtless hollow beneath — and he notes that kneeling with the hands spread is an attitude of prayer figured on the monuments of ancient Egypt. On the opening address he finds the Syriac wording a curious echo of the Lord's Prayer, observes that the Assyrians likewise called their gods without an equal, and reads the phrase about covenant and mercy as a single idea, the covenanted mercy. Clarke adds the Targum's expansion of walking before God with the whole heart: with all the will of their souls and all the affection of their hearts.
16:
The prayer turns from thanksgiving to petition, and Ellicott follows the shift word by word. The opening he renders simply as and now, twice over. What Solomon asks God to keep is the further promise, distinguished from the earlier one whose fulfilment the king has just described. The clause about a successor on the throne he traces through the Greek and Latin versions that the English follows, and the condition attached to it he tightens: not merely yet so that, but only if — a single condition, provided that the sons take heed to their way. The one place where this text departs from the parallel is the phrase in my law, and Ellicott reads the change as the chronicler avoiding an apparent tautology, something he does elsewhere.

On the next verse the variants are smaller but he records them all the same: the Greek and Syriac insert a word of entreaty that the parallel also carries, and where the older book names David as the king's father this one says simply thy servant, to David.

Then comes the question at the heart of the prayer, and both witnesses rise to it. Will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth? Ellicott notes that the Hebrew construction is imitated by the Greek and rendered by the Latin as asking whether such a thing is even credible, and that the words with men are absent from the parallel, the Syriac reading instead with his people. Clarke gives the Targum's expansion in full, and it is the most eloquent thing in the chapter's apparatus: who could have imagined, who could have thought it credible, that God should place his majesty among men dwelling upon earth, when the highest heavens and the middle and the lowest cannot bear the glory of that majesty, nor can this house which I have built contain thee.

After a question of that size the petition that follows is deliberately small, and Ellicott's note registers the change of register rather than resisting it. Turn thou unto thy servant, he would render it, where the English has have respect; and he observes that the parallel adds the word today, which the Greek, Syriac and Arabic supply here as well.
20:
What Solomon asks is that the house should be a direction as much as a dwelling, and Ellicott's notes on these verses keep returning to that idea. The eyes are to be open toward the place; the prayer is to be heard from the dwelling place, from the heavens. He observes that where this text says from, the parallel says unto in both places — an unusual compressed construction that he judges the original. The phrase day and night he marks as the chronicler's substitution of a commoner order for the parallel's night and day.

The direction of prayer he states plainly and without embarrassment: the temple at Jerusalem was, and remains, the point toward which a Jew turns to pray, and he rejects the marginal rendering that would obscure it even though the Syriac, Arabic and Latin support that reading. The word Solomon uses for supplications he notes as chiefly poetic and late, absent from the parallel book altogether and occurring only here in Chronicles, where the older synonym had served before.

Wesley draws out what the petitions assume about prayer itself. Solomon does not ask that God would help his people without their praying for themselves, but that God would help them in answer to their prayers — and Wesley presses the point forward: even the intercession of Christ does not supersede our supplications but encourages them.

The first of the particular cases is the oath sworn at the altar, and here Ellicott has to decide who does what. He reads the neighbour, or people indefinitely, as laying the oath, and the offender as entering upon it before the altar; but he records that all the versions read instead that the man comes and swears there, a difference amounting to one letter prefixed in the Hebrew. Clarke, rather than work through the case, points his reader to his own treatment of the seven cases in the parallel chapter.

Two more notes close the section. Ellicott observes that this chapter says hear from heaven where the parallel omits the preposition and may mean to heaven, and that the chronicler has used the ordinary expression consistently through the cases that follow. And in the clause about requital he prefers the parallel's wording — so as to find guilty — because finding a guilty man guilty balances the justifying of a just one in the clause after it, which the substituted verb does not.
27:
Ellicott is the only witness the catena supplies for this stretch of the prayer, and he reads it as a textual scholar working two manuscripts side by side. The clause asking God to hear he would render as to heaven or in heaven rather than from it, on the pattern of the parallel, while noting that the versions all support the reading the English gives. The clause about teaching is stranger still: the Hebrew here means that God points his people to the good way, a construction found nowhere else, and Ellicott suspects a single particle has been miscopied for another. Correct that, he says, and the verse coincides exactly with its counterpart.

The case of siege gives him more trouble, because the Hebrew as it stands says something odd. The singular and plural shift between the two accounts — an enemy against enemies, him against them — and the phrase describing where the pressure falls reads literally as in the land of his gates. Ellicott sets out what the ancient versions made of it: the Greek has the enemy afflicting the people before their cities, the Latin has the lands laid waste and the gates of the city besieged, the Syriac and Arabic have enemies pressing them hard in their land and in their cities. He inclines, tentatively, to a reading that takes it as in the land at his gates.

Two smaller notes follow. Where this text speaks of a man's own sore and his own grief, the parallel has the plague of his own heart, and Ellicott judges the chronicler's doubled phrase to look like a gloss upon it. And in the verse about God knowing hearts he points out the distributive force of the article — not every man so much as the man, each in his turn — and records that a word meaning all has dropped out of the final clause, as some manuscripts and the versions show. The cumulative effect of these notes is to show a text that has been recopied and lightly reworded rather than freshly composed, which is exactly what the chronicler's method elsewhere would lead a reader to expect.
31:
Ellicott carries this section alone as well, and what he is chiefly tracking is where the chronicler's hand shows. The phrase about walking in God's ways he marks as an explanatory remark added by the later writer rather than drawn from the source. In the verse about the foreigner he finds something rougher: two verses of the older account appear to have been run together here, probably by a copyist's error, which is why the appeal to God's great name arrives without the fuller clause about the mighty hand and the outstretched arm that stands in the parallel.

The smaller variants he records without pressing them. A connecting particle stands here that the parallel omits, though other verses in this same chapter carry it and some manuscripts of the older book do too. The word rendered people he would make plural — the peoples, the nations at large — which matters for a petition about the stranger who comes from far. And a conjunction before the clause about fearing God he would strike, so that the fearing becomes the purpose of the knowing rather than a second item beside it.

Taken together these notes describe a writer working from a source rather than from memory, tidying its grammar where he found it rough and expanding it where he thought it obscure. That is not a criticism in Ellicott's mouth; it is a description of what a compiler does, and it is the reason he is willing to correct this text from the older one at some points and to defend it at others.

Two idioms interest him for their own sake. Praying toward the city is literally praying the way of this city, and the same construction returns further on as the way of their land — a spatial expression doing the work of a preposition. And the petition that God would maintain his people's cause he renders more concretely: that he would do, that is accomplish, their right. The Latin sharpens it further into avenging them, which is a different thing, and Ellicott lets the two stand side by side without choosing.
36:
The last case Solomon puts is captivity, and it opens with the admission that there is no man who does not sin. Clarke does not expound it here, pointing his reader to his fuller treatment in the parallel chapter, and he does the same for the prayer as a whole; what he does supply is the Targum's rendering of the turning-point, that the exiles bethink themselves when the fear of God returns into their hearts.

Ellicott gives the same clause as taking it to heart, and then does something more valuable with the confession that follows. The three verbs are not synonyms, he says, but a climax: we have slipped, or missed the mark; we have done crookedly; we have been godless. Read that way the sentence is a descent rather than a repetition, and he notes the same three verbs standing together in a psalm and in Daniel's prayer.

The verse about the land of captivity he finds corrupt, or at least uncertain. Where this text says the land of their captivity, the parallel says the land of their enemies who carried them captive, and the Syriac says the cities of their captors. Ellicott offers two ways out: either the word for captivity is a corruption of the word for captors, or the relative refers back to the land itself, meaning the hostile nation that carried them off.

Then a plural he distrusts. The word for supplications stands in the singular in the parallel and in several manuscripts and versions; the plural occurs nowhere else and is probably wrong here. And at that point Ellicott marks the most consequential fact about the whole passage: from the clause asking forgiveness for the people onward, the two accounts of Solomon's prayer are wholly dissimilar. What follows is not a variant of the older text but different material altogether.

His notes on that new material are correspondingly close. The request that God's ears be attent means attentive or listening, a word found besides only in one late psalm; the same phrase returns in the next chapter, where the whole verse reappears turned around as a divine promise. And the expression translated the prayer that is made in this place is, in the Hebrew, the prayer of this place — a strange construction occurring only here and in that answering passage.
41:
The prayer ends with words borrowed from a psalm, and Ellicott's business is to show where the borrowing has been altered. The opening connective is the chronicler's addition. The divine title used three times in these two verses appears nowhere else in the prayer, is a favourite of this writer, and is absent from the older book altogether — where the psalm has simply the one name, this text has the compound. The word for resting place is late, occurring besides only in the book of Esther, while the psalm uses the ordinary term. And the closing phrase about rejoicing he calls a paraphrase of the psalm's shout for joy, as the word rendered salvation stands where the psalm had righteousness.

One of those observations is more than lexical, and it puts Ellicott at odds with the other witness here. He judges that the idea of the sanctuary as God's resting place does not sit with the spirit of the prayer, which has insisted throughout that the heaven of heavens cannot contain him and has asked repeatedly that he would hear from heaven, his dwelling place. Wesley reads the same petition in exactly the opposite direction, and paraphrases it warmly: O thou that sittest in the heavens, arise from the throne of thy glory and come down into this place, which thou hast appointed for thy constant habitation, and from which thou wilt not remove as formerly thou hast done. The one takes the phrase as a borrowed formula slightly at odds with its new setting; the other takes it as the point the whole dedication has been working toward.

Clarke supplies the Jewish reading of both closing verses, and it is characteristically concrete. Where the text asks that the saints rejoice in goodness, Jarchi understands the abundance of tithes and other goods given to the Levites as their reward for keeping the ark and singing before it. Where it asks that the face of the anointed not be turned away, Jarchi hears Solomon saying: at least do me good, and if not for my sake, then for thy own. Clarke adds the plain textual fact — these last two verses are absent from the parallel account, and the other differences between the two versions of the prayer are not of much consequence beside that.

Ellicott's last notes bear on how the psalm was reworked. The invocation is used as it is in the priestly blessing; turning away a face means denying a request; and the two halves of the psalm's couplet have been transposed, with the first modified so as to introduce the phrase about the mercies of David — meaning the mercies God promised him. The imperative rendered remember is a form found only here and a handful of times in Nehemiah, which is to say that the prayer closes in the vocabulary of the chronicler's own age rather than Solomon's.
